doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Pressure from a record company, the Steve Allen songs, and Joe Glaser's advice
summary: Bob Thiele pushes commercial songs, and their horror that one might become a hit; lesson to avoid songs they would not be proud of.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: You anticipated my next question. Have you ever been in a situation with a record company where they put significant pressure on you to do something because it’s selling?
Yes.
Yeah, we’ve gotten pressure. Although we haven’t succumbed to it often, but once we had to.
Once we did a thing, it was Bob Thiele, who was with a record company, I don’t remember.
Was it Atlantic?

Whatever. And he said, “listen, you guys have got to cross the line, you’ve got to do something that’s very commercial. You’ve got to do a couple of Steve Allen songs” you’ve got to do this, you’ve got to do that.
Broaden your audience.

Broaden your audience. Okay. We said fine, all right, great. So among other things he gave us one song, he says, “you’ve got to do this.” And it was a song written by Steve Allen called “Pa Take Me to the Circus” built on an old polka melody.
That wasn’t Steve Allen though, honey. Just some other tune that he thought would be a hit.

[humms] In my home town, Czechoslovakian, it’s called “barushka” polka. But this was something else. And we said okay. So we recorded these four things. And later we got home and we sat down and thought about what we did, and actually jumped up in the air in total horror and panic, thinking, what if it becomes popular.
Because we’d have to do it.
What would we do then?
We’d have to do it all the time, oh what did we do?
Oh what have we done?
And that taught us a lesson. Don’t ever do anything that you wouldn’t be proud to do, you know, over and over.
That’s an excellent rule to remember.
Yeah.
Picture doing this on a gig.
Now you’ve got to do it for the rest of your life.
It’s immediate hell.
There’s some more guidance that I guess came through for you. Did it get released?
Yes.
Yeah it was released, but I think it was — was it on vinyl or — I can’t remember was it a 45?
Throw it out of your mind.
It was quite early.
The song that was Steve Allen’s was called “Oh Banana Split.” That was kind of cute.
[humms]

But I mean we would never dream of singing it now, because I mean that was when we were young and you know you could get away with such cutsie pie stuff. But now I mean, I wouldn’t dream of doing it now. But that’s the way the world goes sometimes. Because he was trying to broaden our audience, and we said well okay, maybe this time we’ll try it. But we’d been told stuff a lot of times, even Joe Glaser, who was our booker

at one time early on. We had a meeting with him, he says, “I don’t know, you kids, you walk a line, you’re not cabaret and you’re not jazz, you’re kind of walking the line there. Do one or the other.” We said well this is who we are, this is what we do, this is what we like.
